note: Two fresh instantiations per pattern, in domains other than trading. copied_runs is the longest shared run of consecutive content words against the source excerpts; the build refuses eight or more.

patterns.function: Move the blamed cause onto the thing the writer can change.
patterns.order: scene > winners against losers > not only the obvious cause > but also the controllable one
examples: Some loaves rise and some collapse, and the difference lies not only in the flour but also in how long the dough rests.
Some seedlings thrive and some wilt, and the gap comes not only from the seed but also from the watering schedule.
patterns.appropriate: When the real lever is a decision the writer controls.
patterns.forbidden: When the dismissed cause was never checked.

patterns.function: Announce a count, then name each item with its job.
patterns.order: purpose > count > label and job for each
examples: For the repair we set up two stages: Stage I, finding the leak; Stage II, replacing the pipe.
For the class we planned two drills: Drill I, spelling recall; Drill II, sentence building.
patterns.appropriate: When each item needs both a name and a job.
patterns.forbidden: When the list is bare names with no job.

patterns.function: Set two methods as complements, one covering what the other misses.
patterns.order: method A > the part it handles > the opposite > method B > the other part
examples: We first sand by hand, which smooths the flat faces, and just the opposite, the router shapes the curved edges the hand cannot reach.
We first rinse with cold water, which lifts the loose soil, and just the opposite, the warm soak releases the grit stuck in the seams.
patterns.appropriate: When two methods genuinely cover different parts.
patterns.forbidden: When the two methods do the same job.

patterns.function: Follow a qualitative claim at once with the numbers.
patterns.order: claim > metric > value
examples: The new oven runs far more evenly, with a temperature spread of 3 degrees across the rack.
The repaired pump moves water much faster, with a fill time of 40 seconds for the same tank.
patterns.appropriate: When the number is the one measured.
patterns.forbidden: When the number comes from a different test.

patterns.function: Give a figure, then a second figure, then say which is which.
patterns.order: tool > first value and its time > second value > which-means clause
examples: After curing for a week, the concrete tested at 30 megapascals, which means the strength measured today matches the strength the mix was designed for.
After resting overnight, the dough weighed 900 grams, which means the weight this morning is the same dough that was mixed last night.
patterns.appropriate: When two figures could be confused.
patterns.forbidden: When there is only one figure.

patterns.function: Name the number of parts, then take them in that order.
patterns.order: claim > in N ways > one by > the other by > the parts in order
examples: We checked the roof in two ways, one by spraying water from above and the other by inspecting the beams from below.
We judged the bread in two ways, one by measuring the rise and the other by tasting the crumb.
patterns.appropriate: When the later text follows the announced order.
patterns.forbidden: When the order is announced and then ignored.

patterns.function: End by pointing to another document and listing what it holds.
patterns.order: finally > the document > participle list of its contents
examples: Finally, we left a note for the next shift listing the tasks done, naming the parts replaced, and flagging the leak still open.
Finally, we sent the family a card describing the treatment, explaining the home care, and warning about the side effects.
patterns.appropriate: When the document really contains those items.
patterns.forbidden: When the list invents contents.

patterns.function: Announce a count, name the items, then give the purpose.
patterns.order: count > namely > the items > the purpose
examples: We set aside 3 tools, namely a saw, a plane, and a chisel, hoping to shape the timber with them.
We sowed 3 crops, namely beans, corn, and squash, hoping to feed the bed through summer.
patterns.appropriate: When the count equals the items named.
patterns.forbidden: When the count and the list disagree.

patterns.function: Turn a fact into the question with one 'so'.
patterns.order: fact > so > the question
examples: Bread goes stale because it loses moisture, so how to keep a loaf soft for a week has become the baker's main problem.
Soil packs down under heavy rain, so how to keep a bed loose through winter has become the gardener's main concern.
patterns.appropriate: When the question follows from the fact.
patterns.forbidden: When 'so' joins two unrelated ideas.

patterns.function: Grant the obvious objection before answering it.
patterns.order: of course > blunt judgment
examples: Of course, it is pointless to praise a sauce you have not tasted.
Of course, it is idle to call a joint strong before it has taken any weight.
patterns.appropriate: When the paper then answers the objection.
patterns.forbidden: When the objection is conceded and dropped.

patterns.function: Bring in a second thing as the fix for the first thing's flaw.
patterns.order: however > flaw of the first > the second as remedy
examples: However, because cedar splits along the grain, oak, which holds a screw, is used for the frame instead.
However, because lettuce bolts in heat, chard, which tolerates the sun, is planted beside it.
patterns.appropriate: When the second thing answers the named flaw.
patterns.forbidden: When the second thing is unrelated to the flaw.

patterns.function: State a received principle, then cash it into this decision.
patterns.order: it is often said > example > therefore > the decision
examples: It is often said in the kitchen that a sharp knife is safer than a blunt one, since a blunt edge slips. Therefore, in this class, every station starts with an edge test.
It is often said among builders that a wall is only as straight as its first course. Therefore, on this job, the first course is checked before any more bricks are laid.
patterns.appropriate: When the decision follows from the principle.
patterns.forbidden: When the decision does not follow.

patterns.function: Credit the brief, then list the outputs.
patterns.order: credit > colon > one item per output
examples: Given the client's brief and the limits it sets, we need to deliver the following: a plan, a cost, a schedule, and a handover note.
Given the syllabus and the time allowed, the course has to cover the following: reading, a drill, a test, and a review.
patterns.appropriate: When every item is delivered later.
patterns.forbidden: When an item is listed and never done.

patterns.function: Let a figure carry the overview in one sentence.
patterns.order: one sentence > the figure
examples: The layout of the workshop is shown in Figure 1.
The route of the walk is shown in Figure 2.
patterns.appropriate: When the figure shows the plan.
patterns.forbidden: When the prose also repeats the whole figure.

patterns.function: State an assumption and justify it immediately.
patterns.order: assumption > justification > optional back-reference
examples: Assumption: the oven holds a steady heat. Justification: as noted in the equipment list, the oven has a thermostat.
Assumption: the soil drains freely. Justification: as explained in the site note, the bed sits on a slope.
patterns.appropriate: When the justification gives a reason.
patterns.forbidden: When the justification only repeats the assumption.

patterns.function: Define a term with a colon and a short gloss.
patterns.order: term > colon > definition > character
examples: Proofing: the rest after shaping, during which the dough rises before baking.
Curing: the wait after pouring, during which the concrete hardens before loading.
patterns.appropriate: When the term is used in a special sense.
patterns.forbidden: When the word is ordinary.

patterns.function: Move a long list into a table with one sentence.
patterns.order: one sentence > the table
examples: The tools used at each station are listed in Table 1.
The crops planted in each bed are listed in Table 2.
patterns.appropriate: When the table holds the items.
patterns.forbidden: When the table is missing.

patterns.function: State what is known and wanted, then point to the equation.
patterns.order: known > wanted > the formula is shown in equation N
examples: Knowing the room size, find the paint needed. The formula is shown in equation 1.
Knowing the distance, find the walking time. The formula is shown in equation 2.
patterns.appropriate: When the equation answers the stated need.
patterns.forbidden: When the equation does something else.

patterns.function: Motivate a combination from the mixed character of the subject.
patterns.order: mixed character > so > the combination
examples: The dough needs both stretching and resting, so our method alternates a fold with a pause.
The bed faces both sun and shade, so our planting mixes heat-loving crops with shade crops.
patterns.appropriate: When the combination answers a stated mix.
patterns.forbidden: When a single method would do.

patterns.function: Gloss each symbol with a Where clause.
patterns.order: where > symbol > meaning, repeated
examples: Where w is the width, l is the length, and h is the height.
Where t is the time, d is the distance, and r is the rate.
patterns.appropriate: When every symbol is glossed.
patterns.forbidden: When a symbol is left unexplained.

patterns.function: Turn a diagram into numbered steps.
patterns.order: looking at the figure > N steps > Step 1 action
examples: Looking at the diagram, the assembly splits into 3 steps. Step 1: fix the base to the wall.
Looking at the chart, the recipe splits into 3 steps. Step 1: warm the milk.
patterns.appropriate: When the steps match the figure.
patterns.forbidden: When a step is added that the figure lacks.

patterns.function: Explain a long job by splitting it into small pieces.
patterns.order: long job > by splitting > the consequence
examples: By splitting the renovation into single rooms, we can finish and close one room before opening the next.
By dividing the course into single weeks, we can teach and test one topic before starting the next.
patterns.appropriate: When the split is the one performed.
patterns.forbidden: When the pieces are not the real units.

patterns.function: Report a weakness, then what still holds.
patterns.order: from the figure > weakness > however > remaining strength
examples: From the photo, the finish is not perfectly smooth. However, the joint is still tight and square.
From the tasting, the crumb is not fully even. However, the loaf still rose well and holds its shape.
patterns.appropriate: When both parts are visible.
patterns.forbidden: When the praise contradicts the evidence.

patterns.function: Mark a conclusion as drawn from the evidence, and qualify it.
patterns.order: evidence > therefore we can conclude > qualified conclusion
examples: Therefore, we can conclude that the hand sanding handles the flat surfaces reasonably well.
Therefore, we can conclude that the cold rinse removes the loose dirt reasonably well.
patterns.appropriate: When the qualifier stays in.
patterns.forbidden: When 'reasonably well' is upgraded to 'perfectly'.

patterns.function: Narrate a long procedure with ordinals.
patterns.order: firstly > secondly > thirdly > finally
examples: Firstly, soak the beans; secondly, drain them; thirdly, simmer them; finally, season and serve.
Firstly, cut the boards; secondly, drill the holes; thirdly, glue the joints; finally, clamp and wait.
patterns.appropriate: When the ordinals match the real stages.
patterns.forbidden: When a stage is skipped or renumbered.

patterns.function: Read a result, then give the reason.
patterns.order: by observing the table > finding > this is because > reason
examples: By observing the log, it is not difficult to find that the morning shift finishes faster. This is because the tools are already laid out.
By observing the bed, it is not difficult to find that the east row grows taller. This is because it gets the early sun.
patterns.appropriate: When the reason explains the finding.
patterns.forbidden: When the cause is unrelated.

patterns.function: Name the next part and what carries into it.
patterns.order: therefore > in the next part > what carries forward
examples: Therefore, in the assembly stage, we will use the parts cut in this stage.
Therefore, in the planting stage, we will use the beds prepared in this stage.
patterns.appropriate: When the next part uses that result.
patterns.forbidden: When the next part ignores it.

patterns.function: State a result, then compare it with the alternatives.
patterns.order: result > compared to > the alternatives
examples: The repaired stove boiled the pot in 6 minutes, a clear gain compared with 11 minutes on the old element and 9 on the portable ring.
The new route took 25 minutes, a clear gain compared with 40 minutes by the main road and 33 by the bus.
patterns.appropriate: When the alternatives are the real ones.
patterns.forbidden: When the comparison uses a made-up baseline.

patterns.function: Present an encoded choice as name, role, and table.
patterns.order: label > what it decides > the table
examples: Option A, the wood type, decides which timber enters the frame, and we encode it as shown in the table below.
Option A, the crop choice, decides which plant enters the bed, and we encode it as shown in the table below.
patterns.appropriate: When the table lists the codes.
patterns.forbidden: When the prose describes codes the table lacks.

patterns.function: Decode one code, then say the table covers all cases.
patterns.order: for example > one code > its meaning > coverage claim
examples: For example, if the code is 101, the frame uses oak and steel. It is easy to see that the table covers every combination.
For example, if the code is 110, the bed grows beans and corn. It is easy to see that the table covers every combination.
patterns.appropriate: When the table is genuinely complete.
patterns.forbidden: When a combination is missing.

patterns.function: Concede many options, then justify the single one by a limit.
patterns.order: although many exist > only one is used > since the limit
examples: Although there are many ways to judge a loaf, here only the rise is used, since we can measure only the height.
Although there are many ways to judge a weld, here only the bend is used, since we can test only the flex.
patterns.appropriate: When the limit is real.
patterns.forbidden: When the choice is called best though it is only the available one.

patterns.function: Explain an empty entry so it is not misread.
patterns.order: location > because > reason
examples: In the last column some cells are empty because that station was not running that day.
In the third row some cells are empty because that bed was left fallow that season.
patterns.appropriate: When the reason is true.
patterns.forbidden: When the cell is empty by mistake.

patterns.function: Tie each test to the claim it serves.
patterns.order: to prove the claim > change one thing > change another
examples: To show the joint is sound in both respects, we loaded it in tension and then in shear.
To show the recipe is robust in both respects, we changed the flour and then changed the oven.
patterns.appropriate: When each test bears on the claim.
patterns.forbidden: When a test answers a different question.

patterns.function: Turn a marked picture into a sentence.
patterns.order: as you can see > the behavior
examples: As you can see from the photo, the glue filled the gap along the whole joint.
As you can see from the plot, the plants in the front row grew taller than the back row.
patterns.appropriate: When the picture shows it.
patterns.forbidden: When the sentence adds what the picture lacks.

patterns.function: Turn a comparison into a verdict.
patterns.order: comparison > so > verdict
examples: The original mix set harder than the altered one, so it can be said that the original is the better choice.
The first route stayed drier than the second, so it can be said that the first is the better path.
patterns.appropriate: When the verdict matches the comparison.
patterns.forbidden: When the verdict is stronger than the evidence.

patterns.function: Justify a test by the gap between ideal and real conditions.
patterns.order: good under ideal conditions > but > worse once conditions change
examples: Many glues hold well on a clean bench, but they weaken once the air turns damp.
Many seedlings grow well in a pot, but they struggle once they are moved outside.
patterns.appropriate: When the test then varies that condition.
patterns.forbidden: When the condition is never varied.

patterns.function: Frame a set of scenarios before the table.
patterns.order: to see the impact > we replaced > N scenarios
examples: To see the effect of heat on the set, we replaced the room temperature with the following four settings.
To see the effect of spacing on the yield, we replaced the row gap with the following four distances.
patterns.appropriate: When the table holds those scenarios.
patterns.forbidden: When the count is wrong.

patterns.function: State a conditional result.
patterns.order: we find that > when condition > effect
examples: We find that when the heat is raised on only one side, the joint on that side sets faster.
We find that when the water is cut on only one bed, the plants in that bed wilt first.
patterns.appropriate: When each reading matches one scenario.
patterns.forbidden: When scenarios are merged.

patterns.function: Open a letter in the first person, then move to we.
patterns.order: I am > role > we would like to tell you > topics
examples: I am the person who baked this order. There are a few things we would like to tell you about the ingredients, the method, and the keeping.
I am the carpenter who built this frame. There are a few things we would like to tell you about the timber, the joints, and the finish.
patterns.appropriate: In a letter only.
patterns.forbidden: In the analytical body, which stays in we.

patterns.function: Flag a risk before the caveat.
patterns.order: it is worth noting > risk > the balance
examples: It is worth noting that a sharp chisel cuts cleanly but also bites fast if the hand slips.
It is worth noting that a strong fertilizer pushes growth but also burns the roots if it is overdone.
patterns.appropriate: When the risk is real.
patterns.forbidden: When the caveat is invented.

patterns.function: End a letter with thanks and a wish.
patterns.order: finally > thanks > a wish
examples: Finally, thank you for the order, and we hope the bread keeps well.
Finally, thank you for the work, and we hope the frame serves you for years.
patterns.appropriate: In a letter.
patterns.forbidden: At the end of an analytical section.

patterns.function: Tie a merit to the method that produces it.
patterns.order: by doing > the benefit
examples: By drying the timber before assembly, both warping and shrinkage can be kept in check.
By resting the dough between folds, both strength and extensibility can be built up.
patterns.appropriate: When the merit names its method.
patterns.forbidden: When a benefit is listed with no source.

patterns.function: State a limitation as only, without, so.
patterns.order: only uses > without considering > so > consequence
examples: The method only watches the surface, without considering the moisture inside, so it can only judge the outside.
The test only measures the first day, without considering the weeks after, so it can only speak for the short term.
patterns.appropriate: When the consequence follows.
patterns.forbidden: When the consequence is stronger than the omission.

patterns.function: Frame a recap between a principle and a short verdict.
patterns.order: first of all > the stance > recap > in short > verdict
examples: First of all, we do not assume the weather will cooperate, and we plan for rain. In short, the schedule we set is cautious and workable.
First of all, we do not assume every board is straight, and we check each one. In short, the frame we built is square and sound.
patterns.appropriate: When the verdict matches what was shown.
patterns.forbidden: When the verdict is stronger than the evidence.
